title: Signature Unary Isotope Variations Before Collapse
body:
The Signature isotope variation set is Manon's original design for the narrowest variation class: one element varied only by isotope, with lithium, boron, and silicon as the design's working trio. The design's core is the Signature mass-ladder rule, which ranks isotopes by their mass ratios and assigns each blend a drift score, and the Signature diffusion drift gauge, which predicts how fast a blend separates under a gradient. The design is labeled Signature throughout, so no reader mistakes it for a public measurement: it is a design for organizing isotope variations, with its demo executed at build time.

Variation class. This record covers the Signature unary isotope variation class: one element at a time, varied only by isotope. Its atom types are lithium-6 and lithium-7, boron-10 and boron-11, and silicon-28, silicon-29, and silicon-30. No second element enters this class, which keeps it unary, and the Signature design treats the trio as its ladder: lithium for the largest usable shift, boron for the middle, silicon for the finest.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Signature mass-ladder rule and the Signature diffusion drift gauge. The mass-ladder rule computes each isotope pair's vibrational shift from the mass ratio and ranks the pairs from largest to smallest shift. The drift gauge converts the shift into a separation tendency under a gradient. The demo computes the shifts for lithium-6/7, boron-10/11, and silicon-28/29 from their masses, and its endpoint states the largest shift as the class marker.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for signature unary isotope variations before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: Li-6/7: vibrational shift 7.4%; B-10/11: vibrational shift 4.7%; Si-28/29: vibrational shift 1.7%; ENDPOINT: Signature mass ladder tops at Li-6/7 (7.4%); quantum regime below Debye temperature Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Stability range. The stability range for the Signature isotope set is the whole composition range at ordinary temperatures, because isotopes of one element share bonding and no chemical force separates them. The range holds from cryogenic temperatures up to the element's melting point, and the design's only variation inside it is the drift score, which shrinks as temperature rises and thermal energy swamps the mass differences.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the disappearance of isotope identity as a deciding factor: above the element's Debye temperature, thermal motion washes out zero-point differences, and the blend behaves as a single element with an average mass. At the other extreme, the class stops when the element leaves the condensed state. The demo's endpoint states the lithium shift, the largest in the design's trio, as the threshold marker.

Do not present the Signature mass-ladder rule as a public measurement, and do not use it where a second element enters, because that mixture belongs to a higher-arity class. title: Signature Binary Mixture Architectures Before Collapse
body:
The Signature binary architecture is Manon's original design for two-type mixtures: a pair-balance rule that weighs the unlike interaction against entropy, and a swap gauge that predicts whether a mixture stays mixed or splits. The design takes any pair of atom types, A and B, and returns a critical temperature and a room-temperature split range from a single design interaction strength. It is labeled Signature throughout, so no reader mistakes its design parameters for measured values: the interaction strength is a design input, stated openly in the record.

Variation class. This record covers the Signature binary mixture architecture class: mixtures of exactly two atom types, with no third type present. Its atom types are written generically as A and B, because the class is defined by count, not by chemistry. Chemistry-specific Signature binary families are cross-referenced from their family classes, while this record governs the two-type architecture itself.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Signature pair-balance rule and the Signature swap gauge. The pair-balance rule computes the critical temperature from the design interaction strength and the spinodal compositions at a working temperature. The swap gauge expresses the same result as a tendency: below the critical temperature, swaps that mix the types lose to swaps that separate them. The demo uses a design interaction strength of eight thousand joules per mole.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for signature binary mixture architectures before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Stability range. The stability range for the Signature binary architecture is temperature-dependent: above the critical temperature, the design predicts a single mixed phase in all proportions, and below it, a miscibility gap opens, with only compositions outside the gap staying single-phase. The range is therefore stated as a temperature window, and the demo's critical temperature marks the window's floor.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the critical temperature together with the spinodal compositions at any working temperature. Below the critical temperature, the mixed state inside the gap collapses into two phases at the gap's edge compositions. The demo computes the critical temperature and the room-temperature spinodal for its design interaction, and its endpoint states both as the class threshold.

title: Signature Noble-Gas Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
The Signature noble-gas set is Manon's original design for the inert end of the variation partition: the group-18 elements, helium through radon, mixed under a Signature cross-pair rule that blends pure pair values into cross values with a stated blend factor. The design's point is that inert mixtures need no compound logic at all: with no chemistry to oppose mixing, entropy governs, and the only thresholds are condensation and freezing. It is labeled Signature throughout, so its blend factor is read as a design choice, not a public measurement.

Variation class. This record covers the Signature noble-gas family class: mixtures whose atom types all come from group 18. Its atom types are helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, and radon. No reactive element enters this class, which keeps it the inert anchor of the partition: where reactive Signature classes collapse by compound formation, this class has no compounds to collapse into.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Signature cross-pair rule and the Signature weak-bond gauge. The cross-pair rule takes the geometric mean of two pure energy depths and the arithmetic mean of two pure sizes, then applies a design blend factor of one, keeping the textbook form. The weak-bond gauge reports the cross pair and the mixture's deviation from ideality. The demo computes the helium-neon cross pair from textbook pure values, stated as design inputs.

The range covers every composition from pure helium to pure radon, limited at the top by temperature and pressure rather than by chemistry.

It is labeled Signature throughout, so its design parameters are read as design inputs, not measured values.

title: Signature Alkaline-Earth Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
The Signature alkaline-earth set is Manon's original design for group-2 mixtures: beryllium through barium, judged by a Signature size-strain gauge against calcium as the middle reference. The design's point is that group 2 spans a wide size range, so neighbors mix and distant cousins split, and calcium as reference shows the pattern symmetrically: beryllium and magnesium fail below, strontium and barium pass above. It is labeled Signature throughout, so its model radii are read as design inputs, not crystal measurements.

Variation class. This record covers the Signature alkaline-earth family class: mixtures whose atom types all come from group 2. Its atom types are beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, and barium. The class is disjoint from the alkali class by group membership: a mixture belongs here exactly when all its types are alkaline-earth metals, with calcium as the design's reference.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Signature size-strain gauge and the Signature pair-balance rule. The size-strain gauge compares each member's radius against calcium and flags pairs beyond fifteen percent. The pair-balance rule gives miscibility gaps from a design interaction strength for pairs that pass the gauge. The demo applies the size-strain gauge against calcium with model radii stated in the record.

The Signature light-element set is Manon's original design for the low-atomic-number class: hydrogen through neon, judged by a Signature size-strain gauge against beryllium as reference and a reactivity gauge that flags pairs likely to compound. Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Signature size-strain gauge and the Signature reactivity gauge. The size-strain gauge compares each member's radius against beryllium and flags pairs beyond fifteen percent. body:

The Signature transition-metal set is Manon's original design for the d-block: scandium through mercury, judged by a Signature size-strain gauge against nickel as reference and a d-band gauge that tracks how band filling shifts with composition. The design's point is the d-block's breadth: neighbors mix broadly, distant members split, and nickel as reference shows a different pass-fail map than iron, with silver and gold failing where they pass against other solvents. It is labeled Signature throughout, so its model radii are read as design inputs.

Variation class. This record covers the Signature transition-metal family class: mixtures whose atom types all come from the d-block. Its atom types are scandium, titanium, vanadium, chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel, copper, zinc, yttrium, zirconium, niobium, molybdenum, technetium, ruthenium, rhodium, palladium, silver, cadmium, hafnium, tantalum, tungsten, rhenium, osmium, iridium, platinum, gold, and mercury. The class is disjoint from the other families by block position: a mixture belongs here exactly when all its types are transition metals, with nickel as the design's reference.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Signature size-strain gauge and the Signature d-band gauge. The size-strain gauge compares each member's radius against nickel and flags pairs beyond fifteen percent. The d-band gauge tracks how d-band filling shifts with composition, which governs magnetism and bonding in the design. The demo applies the size-strain gauge against nickel with model radii for the full d-block.

Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The range is therefore stated per pair against the solvent, and the demo's table is the range for nickel-based mixtures.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the fifteen-percent size rule for solid solutions together with the ordering threshold for pairs that prefer an ordered compound over a disordered solution. Beyond the size limit, the mixture collapses into separate crystals; where ordering wins, it collapses into an ordered phase. The demo's endpoint states the size-strain verdicts against nickel.

title: Signature Lanthanide Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
The Signature lanthanide set is Manon's original design for the rare-earth row: lanthanum through lutetium, judged by a Signature size-strain gauge against lutetium as the end reference and a contraction gauge that tracks the steady radius shrink. The design's point is the contraction's consequence: even the largest lanthanide sits within fifteen percent of the smallest, so the whole row passes the gauge, and the class's collapse threshold is rarely reached among lanthanides themselves. It is labeled Signature throughout, so its model radii are read as design inputs.

Variation class. This record covers the Signature lanthanide family class: mixtures whose atom types all come from the lanthanide row. Its atom types are lanthanum, cerium, praseodymium, neodymium, promethium, samarium, europium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, holmium, erbium, thulium, ytterbium, and lutetium. The class is disjoint from the other families by row membership: a mixture belongs here exactly when all its types are lanthanides, with lutetium as the design's reference.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Signature size-strain gauge and the Signature contraction gauge. The size-strain gauge compares each member's radius against lutetium and flags pairs beyond fifteen percent. The contraction gauge tracks the steady shrink across the row, which is why the gauge passes throughout. The demo applies the size-strain gauge against lutetium with model radii for the full row.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for signature lanthanide mixtures before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: La: mismatch vs Lu 8.1% PASS; Ce: mismatch vs Lu 5.2% PASS; Pr: mismatch vs Lu 5.2% PASS; Nd: mismatch vs Lu 4.6% PASS; Pm: mismatch vs Lu 4.0% PASS; Sm: mismatch vs Lu 4.0% PASS; Eu: mismatch vs Lu 14.5% PASS; Gd: mismatch vs Lu 2.9% PASS; Tb: mismatch vs Lu 2.3% PASS; Dy: mismatch vs Lu 2.3% PASS; Ho: mismatch vs Lu 1.7% PASS; Er: mismatch vs Lu 1.2% PASS; Tm: mismatch vs Lu 0.6% PASS; Yb: mismatch vs Lu 12.1% PASS; Lu: mismatch vs Lu 0.0% PASS; ENDPOINT: Signature size-strain 15% rule vs Lu; contraction keeps all pairs passing Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Stability range. The stability range for the Signature lanthanide set is broad across the whole row: because contraction keeps sizes close, lanthanides mix in broad proportions, and the design's mixed rare-earth alloy spans the light half of the row. The range is therefore stated as broad for the full row, with europium and ytterbium as the mild exceptions, since their divalent character makes them larger than the trend, though still passing against lutetium.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the fifteen-percent size rule, which lanthanides almost never cross against each other, together with the compound-formation threshold where a lanthanide prefers an ordered compound over a solution. The class's honest result is that its collapse threshold is rarely reached among lanthanides themselves: the mixture usually survives, and collapse arrives from outside, through oxidation or through a non-lanthanide partner. The demo's endpoint states the size-strain verdicts against lutetium.

Use and limits. Use this record for Signature mischmetal, magnet-alloy, and phosphor designs, and as the f-row anchor of the Signature family partition. Do not present model radii as exact values, and do not confuse broad lanthanide mixing with easy separation, because separation is hard precisely because the members are so similar. title: Signature Heavy-Element Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
The Signature heavy-element set is Manon's original design for the high-atomic-number class: hafnium through bismuth, judged by a Signature squeeze-collapse gauge that compares a model open structure against a model dense structure under pressure. The design's point is pressure-driven structural collapse: squeezing forces one crystal structure to give way to a denser one, and the gauge returns the pressure where the dense structure wins. It is labeled Signature throughout, so its equation-of-state parameters are read as design inputs, not measured values.

Variation class. This record covers the Signature heavy-element range class: mixtures whose atom types all have atomic number seventy-two or above, capped at bismuth. Its atom types are hafnium, tantalum, tungsten, rhenium, osmium, iridium, platinum, gold, mercury, thallium, lead, and bismuth. The class is defined by its atomic-number floor and its bismuth cap, which keeps it disjoint from the light-element range class.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Signature squeeze-collapse gauge and the Signature size-strain gauge. The squeeze-collapse gauge computes energy against volume for each structure and finds their enthalpy crossing under pressure. The size-strain gauge tests solid solubility against the fifteen-percent rule. The demo compares a model crystal structure against a model dense structure with design parameters distinct from the public edition's.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for signature heavy-element mixtures before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: collapse pressure: 0.0690 eV/A^3 = 11.1 GPa; ENDPOINT: dense structure wins above 11.1 GPa; open structure collapses Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Stability range. The stability range for the Signature heavy-element set is broad at ordinary pressure for neighbors and narrow for distant pairs, and it narrows further under pressure, because squeezing favors the densest structure regardless of mixing. Tungsten-rhenium and platinum-iridium mix broadly in the design, while lead-bismuth forms a eutectic coolant. The range is therefore stated as a pressure window plus per-pair solubilities.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the pressure where the dense structure's enthalpy falls below the open structure's enthalpy, together with the fifteen-percent size rule for solid solutions. Beyond the pressure threshold, the mixture's structure collapses into the denser phase, and beyond the size limit, it splits into separate crystals. The demo's endpoint states the structural collapse pressure for its design pair.

Use and limits. Use this record for Signature heavy-alloy, shielding, and coolant designs, and as the high-mass anchor of the Signature range partition. Do not present design equation-of-state parameters as measured values, and do not use the design for mixtures outside the hafnium-to-bismuth range. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

def E(V, E0, V0, B0, Bp):
    eta = (V0 / V) ** (2.0 / 3.0)
    return E0 + (9 * V0 * B0 / 16) * ((eta - 1) ** 2 * Bp + (eta - 1) ** 2 * (6 - 4 * eta))
CR = (-13.0, 100.0, 0.75, 4.0)
AM = (-12.4, 92.0, 0.45, 4.0)
cross = None
P = 0.001
while P < 0.150:
    Vc = CR[1] * (1 - P / (3 * CR[2]))
    Va = AM[1] * (1 - P / (3 * AM[2]))
    Hc = E(Vc, *CR) + P * Vc
    Ha = E(Va, *AM) + P * Va
    if Ha < Hc:
        cross = P
        break
    P += 0.001
print('collapse pressure: %.4f eV/A^3 = %.1f GPa' % (cross, cross * 160.2))
print('ENDPOINT: dense structure wins above %.1f GPa; open structure collapses' % (cross * 160.2))

title: Signature Hydrogen-Bearing Mixtures Before Collapse
body:
The Signature hydrogen-bearing set is Manon's original design for the interstitial class: hydrogen dissolved in palladium, iron, titanium, zirconium, magnesium, or nickel, judged by a Signature dissolve gauge and a hydride-win rule. The design's point is hydrogen's unique role: small enough to sit in the gaps between host atoms, fast enough to diffuse anywhere, and dangerous enough to crack the host when it forms a hydride. It is labeled Signature throughout, so its dissolve constant and threshold are read as design inputs.

Variation class. This record covers the Signature hydrogen-bearing special class: mixtures of hydrogen with a host metal. Its atom types are hydrogen, palladium, iron, titanium, zirconium, magnesium, and nickel, in pairs or groups where hydrogen is the dissolved partner and the metal is the host. The class is defined by hydrogen's interstitial role: a mixture belongs here exactly when hydrogen enters the gaps of a host lattice rather than replacing host atoms.

Mixing algorithms. The mixing algorithms for this class are the Signature dissolve gauge and the Signature hydride-win rule. The dissolve gauge gives dissolved hydrogen concentration as proportional to the square root of hydrogen pressure, with a design constant. The hydride-win rule declares a hydride winner whenever the dissolved concentration reaches the design threshold. The demo applies the dissolve gauge with a design constant of three hundredths and a design hydride threshold of twelve hundredths.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record computes the class threshold for signature hydrogen-bearing mixtures before collapse. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: p=0.01 bar: dissolved H=0.003 dissolved; p=0.10 bar: dissolved H=0.009 dissolved; p=1.00 bar: dissolved H=0.030 dissolved; p=4.00 bar: dissolved H=0.060 dissolved; p=16.00 bar: dissolved H=0.120 HYDRIDE; ENDPOINT: hydride collapse threshold p*=16.0 bar at design K Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Stability range. The stability range for the Signature hydrogen-bearing set is the dissolved window: below the hydride threshold concentration, hydrogen stays dissolved and the host keeps its structure, while the window's width depends on the host, with palladium dissolving the most and iron the least at ordinary pressure. The range is therefore stated as a pressure window per host, from trace dissolution up to the hydride threshold, and the demo's threshold pressure marks the window's top for its design parameters.

Collapse threshold. The collapse threshold for this class is the hydride threshold concentration: beyond it, the dissolved mixture collapses into a hydride phase, which is brittle and often cracks the host, and the collapse is the embrittlement failure mode that hydrogen safety design exists to prevent. The threshold is reached by raising pressure, lowering temperature, or both, and the demo computes the threshold pressure for its design constant. The demo's endpoint states that pressure as the class threshold.

Use and limits. Use this record for Signature hydrogen-storage, fuel-cell, pipeline, and pressure-vessel designs, and as the interstitial anchor of the Signature partition. Do not present the design dissolve constant or threshold as measured values for a real host, and do not ignore embrittlement where hydrogen meets stressed steel.
